rows.subtype: Approach: designs a team project by listing how it would fall apart [Action]
rows.description: A student team lists what would spoil their project: unclear roles, last-minute merging, one person unreachable. They set roles, weekly merges and a shared contact sheet.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: only avoids bad outcomes and never defines a positive goal [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student who avoids every mistake he can think of ends up with a safe, empty plan. Avoiding failure is not the same as working toward something wanted.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: asks how to make a situation worse to spot hidden levers [Thinking]
rows.description: A manager with a noisy meeting culture asks what would make it worse and notes late agendas and no notes. Fixing those two makes meetings shorter and calmer.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: pairs the list of things to avoid with a positive target [Revision]
rows.description: Noticing the plan is only defensive, she adds one clear aim per month, so avoidance rules serve a direction rather than becoming the whole plan.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: keeps asking why until a deeper cause appears [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl keeps losing her pencil box. Why? Left at school. Why? Rushed at bell. Why? Packing after the bell. So she starts packing five minutes before it.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: traces a repeated problem to its underlying cause [Thinking]
rows.description: A student failing maths tests asks why: careless errors, because rushed, because time ran out, because early questions were slow. The fix is practising early topics for speed.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: acts on the root cause found rather than the symptom [Action]
rows.description: A hostel student late every morning traces it to poor sleep, then to late phone use, then to a habit of scrolling. He charges the phone outside the room.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: stops at a convenient answer and blames a person [Pitfall]
rows.description: After a software outage, a team asks why once and says a colleague made a mistake. The deeper causes, missing tests and unclear review, remain and the outage recurs.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: continues asking until a process cause appears and fixes the process [Revision]
rows.description: The team revisits the outage and asks why five times. They find a missing check in deployment and add an automated test rather than assigning blame.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: shouts out many ideas together before choosing one [Thinking]
rows.description: Asked how to decorate the classroom for a festival, children call out flowers, lamps, paper chains and rangoli. The teacher writes all of them, then the class votes for two.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
